The album for Ludwig
In June, Ludwig turns 80. Mara and Lena are secretly putting together a photo album. They're sitting at the table in the bakery, after closing time, with hundreds of photos.
Look, this photo! It's the day Grandpa drove his first tram. 1968.
He looks so young! And who's the woman standing next to him?
That's his mother. The woman who cooked sarmale (cabbage rolls) without meat after the war.
And this one? The man with the long hair and the guitar?
That's Grandpa too! With the band that was called “The Rails”. And the woman sitting at the back with the book is Grandma Ingrid.
With the book! At a rock concert! That's the photo he told me about.
Exactly. What do we write under each photo? I'd like short captions that make him laugh.
How about: “The man who never had to brake, because everyone else braked”?
Ha! Perfect. And under the photo of Fritz: “The dog nobody is allowed to give sausage to, and who still always gets some.”
And the last photo? The one where we're all in the courtyard, at the party?
Underneath we write: “The people you're there for every day. And who are now there for you.”
Lena, I think it's the most beautiful album I've ever seen. He's going to cry.
He'll say it's just the dust. As always.

1. What a relative clause is

A relative clause describes a noun, like “who / which / that” in English. The relative pronoun looks like the definite article (der, die, das), and the conjugated verb goes to the END. There is ALWAYS a comma before it:
The woman who plays the piano is 91. (relative clause in the middle of the sentence: a comma after it too)
2. The gender and case of the pronoun
The GENDER and NUMBER come from the noun being described. The CASE comes from the pronoun's role in the relative clause:
denen (!)
Genitive
dessen
deren
the dog that barks (subject → Nom.)
the dog that Kuba adopted (direct object → Akk.)
the dog nobody is allowed to give sausage to (Dat.)
the children the dog belongs to (Dat. plural)
Ask yourself the question inside the relative clause: who does it? (Nom.), whom? (Akk.), to whom? (Dat.), whose? (Gen.).
3. With a preposition
If the verb in the relative clause needs a preposition, the preposition goes BEFORE the pronoun, with the case it requires:
This is the woman I work with.
This is the friend I'm waiting for. (warten auf + Akk.)
This is the photo he told me about.
In German, the preposition can't go at the end of the clause (as in English “the house I live in”). It always goes before the relative pronoun.
4. Wo and was
For places (cities, countries, or instead of “in dem”) you can use “wo”:
Berlin is the city where I work.
After “alles, nichts, etwas, vieles, das” and after superlatives used as nouns, you use “was”:
There's nothing he can't repair.
It's the most beautiful thing I've ever seen.
The woman who plays the piano is called Margarete.
This is the child I helped. (helfen + Dat.)
These are the neighbours we celebrate with.
The film I saw yesterday was good.

Achtzig Jahre

Ludwig's eightieth birthday fell on a Saturday in June, right when the lime trees were in blossom and the whole of Berlin smells of honey. Ludwig had said he didn't want to celebrate. “Eighty is no reason to celebrate,” he had said. “Eighty is a reason to go to bed early.” Nobody had believed him.

In the morning he went as usual at seven with Fritz to the bakery to get his two bread rolls. The bakery was closed. On the door hung a note that Lena had written: “Closed today because of a very important birthday. Please go to the courtyard.”

Fifty people were standing in the courtyard. Under the chestnut tree, in which the fairy lights were hanging again, there was a long table with a white tablecloth. On it was a huge cake, which Lena had baked all night, in the shape of a yellow tram, with eighty little candles on the roof. When Ludwig walked into the courtyard, everyone started singing. And at a window on the fourth floor, a piano began to play.

Everyone who meant something to Ludwig was there. The Nowak family with Kuba, Ola and Bruno, who was wearing a bow round his neck that he liked as little as Fritz once had. Klaus, the beekeeper, who had been playing chess with Ludwig for fifty years and still beat him every week. Mr Wolff, the trainee who never knew how to brake, in his uniform. Dr Yılmaz with her guitar. And Jonas and Clara, who had just come back from Romania and looked tanned.

But there was one more surprise, which not even Lena knew about. At the courtyard gate, a little behind the others, stood a man of about fifty, tall and grey-haired, with three young people beside him. Ludwig saw him and stopped.
Thomas?

It was his son, who lived in Munich and whom he hadn't seen for three years. After Ingrid's death they had quarrelled, over things neither of them could quite remember any more. After that they had only spoken briefly on the phone, at Christmas and on birthdays. Since the first video call in the winter, in which Ludwig had shown only his nose, they had been talking more often again. But they hadn't seen each other.
Hello, Dad. Happy birthday. Mara wrote to me. She said it was a party the whole family should be at.

Ludwig said nothing. He walked slowly to the gate, without his stick, and hugged his son. For a long time. The three grandchildren, whom he had last seen as children and who were now almost adults, stood awkwardly beside them. The youngest, Paul, fourteen, had a guitar on his back. “Grandpa,” he said shyly, “Dad said you used to play in a band. Can you teach me something?”

Mara was standing next to Lena and holding her hand. Lena was crying. She hadn't known that Mara had written to her uncle. “It's the most beautiful thing you've ever done,” she whispered. Mara shook her head. “He wanted to come. He just didn't know how. Sometimes you need someone to open the door a little.”

An hour later, Mara found father and son in Ludwig's kitchen, at the little table where Ludwig ate his bread rolls every morning. They were drinking coffee from the old cups with blue flowers that Ingrid had bought fifty years ago. Thomas held his hands around the cup, exactly the way his father always did. Mara stopped in the doorway and wanted to slip away quietly, but she still heard what Thomas said: “Dad, I don't know any more why we quarrelled back then. I only know Mum would have been sad.” Ludwig didn't answer straight away. Then he said: “Your mother always said we were both too stubborn. That we're more alike than we want to admit.” Thomas laughed quietly. “She was right most of the time.” — “Not most of the time,” said Ludwig. “Always.”

Later, after the cake had been eaten and the eighty candles had been blown out, which cost Ludwig three attempts and the help of all the children, Lena gave him the album. Ludwig slowly leafed through the pages. The photo from 1968, in which he was standing in front of his first tram. The photo in which Ingrid sat at the back with her book, in the cellar. The photo from the courtyard party, under which it said: “The people you're there for every day. And who are now there for you.”

Ludwig closed the album. He took off his glasses and wiped them for a long time with his handkerchief. “The dust,” he said. “From the old photos.” And everyone standing around him nodded seriously and pretended to believe him.

Then Clara stood up and tapped her glass with a teaspoon. “We have a surprise too,” she said and took Jonas by the hand. “In Romania we didn't just see monasteries and mountains. We also brought something back with us.” She put her hand on her belly. “In December we're having a baby. And we'd like to ask Mara if she wants to be the godmother. The woman without whom we would never have got engaged.”

The courtyard exploded with joy. Kuba and Ola danced with the dogs. Mrs Hoffmann played a waltz at the open window. Ludwig picked up his guitar, Paul his, and for the first time in decades two Brandts played together, one old and one young, under a chestnut tree that had already stood there when Ludwig himself was a boy dreaming of Elvis.
Fritz and Bruno lay under the table and slept, side by side, two old dogs who had celebrated enough. Above them, on the first floor, the yellow lamp was on, even though it was still light.
Thomas stayed in Berlin for three days. On the last evening he said: “Next year we'll come again. And we'll all celebrate Christmas together, here, under the yellow lamp.”
